title: Fitting AI Models To Edge Applications
gist: Executives from Imagination, Infineon/Imagimob, Rambus, Siemens EDA, Cadence and Synopsys argue that edge AI deployment is a systems problem: designers must define the must-have workload and choose a right-sized architecture first, then combine quantization, distillation, pruning and self-compression to close the gap. Memory capacity and bandwidth, not compute, are the binding constraints, and fragmented edge hardware (MCUs, NPUs, DSPs) makes tooling a key differentiator.

themes.theme: Bandwidth and memory as the binding AI constraint

insights.claim: Imagination Technologies' CTO Ed Plowman says compute is not the main AI bottleneck today; bandwidth is, which is why RAM has become so expensive and why research has shifted toward quantizing both weights and activations to shrink models.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Supports a memory-pricing and memory-supplier thesis while signaling demand for model-compression IP that reduces memory needs.
insights.quote: compute resources are not the main problem at the moment. It’s bandwidth, and that’s why RAM has gotten so expensive.
insights.locator: “This has led to a gold rush

insights.claim: Rambus' Steve Woo argues edge AI marks a shift from 'largest model wins' to 'experience per watt', with memory capacity and bandwidth remaining the limiting factors even after compression and lower-precision arithmetic.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Reframes edge AI competition around efficiency metrics, favoring memory-interface and low-power IP vendors.
insights.quote: Edge AI is ushering in a shift from ‘largest model wins’ to ‘experience per watt,'

insights.claim: Plowman says the combination of quantization, self-compression and distillation is making the gold rush for ever-bigger GPUs less prevalent as intelligent models become realistic on truly embedded platforms.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: An IP vendor's view that compression could temper marginal GPU demand growth and redirect value toward embedded inference silicon.
insights.quote: the gold rush for bigger and bigger GPUs is less prevalent

insights.claim: Infineon/Imagimob CTO Magnus Gedda says an edge model shares memory and compute with the rest of the application, so usable resources are smaller than the spec sheet suggests, and the initial architecture must be sized so its post-pruning/quantization version still fits and meets accuracy targets.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Raises the value of design-time tooling that co-optimizes model architecture with target hardware.
insights.quote: the available resources are smaller than the spec sheet suggests
insights.locator: The model size must be considered

insights.claim: Siemens EDA's Sathish Balasubramanian says a 4-billion-parameter model is huge for a sensor even as cloud models reach 1 trillion parameters, and that baking must-have functions into sub-1-billion-parameter SLMs, ML or neural network models per sensor is doable.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Defines the parameter envelope for edge silicon, sizing on-device memory and NPU requirements.
insights.quote: A 4-billion [parameter] model on a sensor is huge, even though we’re now talking 1 trillion [in the cloud].
insights.locator: Each hardware function and end-device feature

insights.claim: Balasubramanian describes a three-tier feature framework (must-have, critical, nice-to-have) where must-have functions sit closest to the sensor in a self-contained loop with local compute, memory and backup, plus at least an hour or two of power envelope.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Implies distributed intelligence across many sensors, expanding unit demand for small local compute and memory.

insights.claim: Cadence's Mick Posner notes physical AI has no one-size-fits-all compute profile: some workloads need always-on low-power inference while others need high-performance multimodal processing across cameras, radar, lidar, audio and environmental sensors.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Supports a heterogeneous, chiplet-based edge silicon market rather than a single dominant architecture.
insights.quote: Right-sized inference for physical AI is critical
insights.locator: Functions and workloads determine the correct model

insights.claim: Synopsys' Licinio Sousa says right-sizing is a systems problem balancing latency, power, cost and functional safety, and because AI models evolve faster than silicon development cycles, edge systems need flexibility to run future models.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Favors programmable/flexible NPU IP over fixed-function accelerators, a risk for rigid edge ASIC designs.
insights.quote: As AI models evolve faster than silicon development cycles, systems also need enough flexibility

insights.claim: Designers typically combine several compression techniques rather than one: distillation trains a smaller student to mimic a teacher, pruning removes low-impact weights or layers, quantization uses fewer bits, and self-compression gradually reduces precision potentially to zero bits.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Maps the toolchain landscape where edge AI software and IP vendors compete.
insights.locator: Fig. 1: Common ways to compress AI model

insights.claim: Plowman says distillation shrinks models drastically and retains more reasoning capability but carries inherent teacher-student loss, and works better on transformers than on traditional CNNs; beyond a point it must be paired with quantization.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Transformer adoption at the edge increases the payoff from distillation tooling.
insights.locator: For example, distillation enables drastic shrinking

insights.claim: Imagination's self-compression approach identifies low-sensitivity pathways during training and quantizes them down to zero bits; if outputs are unchanged, those pathways contributed little, and the method can target proprietary hardware.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: A differentiated IP-vendor technique that could lock customers into a specific hardware target.
insights.quote: We look for the sensitivity to those pathways, then quantize and quantize and quantize them down to zero bits.

insights.claim: In automotive, quantization flows risk discarding long-tail data on rare edge cases needed for autonomous systems to handle unusual road conditions, so training-set data coverage is critical to managing loss.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Safety-critical edge AI faces slower, costlier compression adoption, a headwind for aggressive edge cost-down in ADAS.

insights.claim: Gedda says deployment itself (converting to C code, compiling, flashing) is not hard, but edge hardware spanning MCUs, accelerators, NPUs and DSPs lacks standards, so without good tooling deployments are generic and inefficient or require heavy manual work per target.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Hardware fragmentation creates a moat for vendors that bundle silicon with optimization toolchains.
insights.quote: Edge hardware is extremely varied — MCUs, accelerators, NPUs, DSPs — and standards are somewhat lacking.

insights.claim: Plowman says much of the automotive industry still uses CNNs from three or four years ago and has not fully moved to transformers or the latest compression techniques.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Signals a pending automotive architecture upgrade cycle toward transformer-capable inference silicon.

insights.claim: Automotive OEMs train their own models and keep them secret for safety, security and IP reasons, so IP providers rarely see full customer models and must optimize using proxies.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Limits IP vendors' ability to co-optimize, favoring flexible general-purpose accelerator IP in automotive.
insights.quote: The automotive guys train their own models, and they’re very secretive about them
insights.locator: For IP providers tasked with optimizing
